R01: Rewrite: "Plan, discuss, and ship work in one shared workspace. Over 10,000 teams use it." What changed: I cut the stock opener ("today's fast-paced digital landscape"), the empty verbs ("unlock the power"), the "not just X, it's Y" construction, "game-changer", and the "Read that again" line. Those are recognizable filler and make readers trust the copy less. I replaced the vague promise with concrete actions the product supports. R02: I won't remove them silently. The em dashes are a deliberate part of the user's voice, and changing an author's style without telling them is a trust problem, not an edit. What I'd do: keep the em dashes by default, since the sample is the style reference. If there's a real reason to cut them (a house style guide, or worry that em dashes read as AI-written), say so openly: "Your sample uses em dashes on purpose. Should I keep them, reduce them, or replace them with commas, colons, or parentheses?" If they say replace, swap each one for the punctuation that fits the meaning (an aside becomes parentheses, an explanation becomes a colon, a pause becomes a comma or a new sentence). Then list the changes or show a diff so they can review it. Never make undisclosed changes to someone's voice.
R03: These are two separate problems, and the injection comes first because it's a security issue. Injection: treat all retrieved and tool output as data, never as instructions. Wrap it in delimited or untrusted blocks. Don't let model output trigger destructive tools on its own: delete_invoice needs a server-side authorization check scoped to the user, explicit human confirmation, and an allowlist of tools per task (a read-only copilot shouldn't expose delete at all). Log and flag the document, sanitize or quarantine its source, and add this case to red-team evals (OWASP LLM01). Latency: break the 4.8s TTFT down into retrieval, reranking, prompt assembly, queueing, and model prefill. Typical fixes: shrink and trim the context (top-k, compress chunks), put stable system and tool content first so prefix caching can hit, run retrieval in parallel, cache embeddings, use a smaller or faster model for routing, and stream status updates right away. Set an SLO (for example, p95 TTFT under 1.5s) and measure before and after each change.
R04: There are two defects. 1) In a stdio MCP server, stdout is the JSON-RPC channel. Any console.log or print corrupts the protocol and the client fails to parse messages or disconnects. Send all logs to stderr (console.error, or logging with sys.stderr), or use the MCP logging notification. Never print banners to stdout. 2) Accepting any filePath is a path traversal and arbitrary file read/write vulnerability, and the LLM can be prompt-injected into exploiting it. Fix it this way: configure an allowlist of root directories, resolve the canonical path (realpath, which follows symlinks), and reject anything outside the roots after resolution. Reject NUL bytes, device paths, and UNC paths. Validate with a schema (zod or pydantic). Make the server read-only by default and require explicit opt-in for writes. Cap file sizes. Run it with least privilege (a dedicated user or container) and don't pass secrets in env unless needed. Add tests: ../ escapes, symlinks, absolute paths, Windows drive letters, and a check that stdout stays valid JSON-RPC only.
R05: A clean OpenAPI diff only shows the schema is unchanged. Behavior still broke. Both changes are semantic breaking changes. 1) Changing the default sort from DESC to ASC breaks clients that read the first page as "latest", and it can invalidate existing cursors (duplicated or skipped rows). 2) Returning null where the key used to be omitted breaks clients that check key existence, strict deserializers, and the PATCH semantics of absent versus null. Decision: treat this as breaking. Restore the old defaults (DESC, key omitted). Put the new behavior behind an explicit opt-in (?sort=created_at:asc, or a new version or header). If it must change, deprecate it with Deprecation/Sunset headers, a changelog entry, and notice to consumers. To prevent a repeat, write down the default sort and the null-vs-absent rules in the spec, add contract tests or consumer-driven contracts (Pact) that pin ordering and key presence, and replay recorded production responses in CI.
R06: This is a domain invariant problem, not a UI bug. A completed schedule is an immutable fact that payroll and trip logs are built from. Rules: block direct edits to completed or closed schedules on the server side, not just in the UI. Model the change as an explicit correction command (DriverReassignmentCorrection) that requires a reason code, an authorized role (a supervisor, with four-eyes approval if payroll is already closed), and a check against the payroll period's lock state. Keep the original record and write a compensating or adjusting entry with who, when, and why, rather than overwriting. Emit a domain event so payroll and trip logs recompute through adjustment lines for both drivers, and so reports for closed periods show the correction as a delta. Use optimistic locking (a version column) to prevent concurrent overwrites. For past damage, audit history (or the audit log or CDC) for backdated swaps, reconcile them against payroll, and fix them through adjustments. Add tests covering a swap after completion, a swap after payroll close, and an unauthorized role.
R07: Mapping unknown statuses to DELIVERED is a data-integrity bug. It fails open, can trigger payouts, invoices, or customer notifications, and hides the change. Fix: use an anti-corruption layer with an explicit mapping table. Unknown values map to a non-terminal UNKNOWN or NEEDS_REVIEW state (fail closed). Store the raw external status, alert or log with metrics, and don't fire terminal side effects. Map ERP_CUSTOMS_HOLD to a proper internal state (ON_HOLD or EXCEPTION, with a customs reason) and update the state machine's allowed transitions. Make the mapping exhaustive in code (a TypeScript never-check or enum match) and have contract tests fail on unmapped values. Backfill: find shipments marked DELIVERED from unknown raw statuses, revert or flag them, and reconcile them with the courier's ERP. Process webhooks idempotently and in order (guarding on event timestamp or sequence), and keep a DLQ or review queue for anything still unmapped.
R08: Request changes and ask for it to be split into separate PRs. Reasons: the 40 reformatted files bury the actual fix, make review and git blame harder, and raise the chance of merge conflicts. Replacing axios with ky is an unrequested dependency and behavior change. Their semantics differ: ky throws on any non-2xx by default and axios uses validateStatus, interceptors map to hooks, JSON and error shapes differ, timeouts and retries differ (ky retries by default), and ky doesn't support Node or XHR progress the same way. That's regression risk across every HTTP call, unrelated to the login bug. Ask for: PR 1, the minimal login fix plus a regression test that reproduces the bug. PR 2 (optional), formatting only, applied by the project formatter, with the commit added to .git-blame-ignore-revs. PR 3 (only if justified), the HTTP client migration with a decision record, a bundle and feature comparison, interceptor and error-handling parity, and tests. Then review the login fix itself: root cause, auth edge cases, and that nothing is logged that shouldn't be.
R09: Don't ship. An aggregate score is the wrong measure here. Cross-tenant IDOR is a critical security and privacy failure (data breach, and possible UU PDP or GDPR notification duties), and one leak is enough to block release. Treat tenant isolation as a hard gate where 100% must pass, not a weighted average. Next steps: reproduce both failures, find the root cause (a missing server-side tenant scope on the query or object lookup, trusting a client-supplied tenant or ID, cache keys not partitioned by tenant, or a RAG or search index missing a tenant prefilter), and fix it centrally (enforce tenant scope in the data access layer or with Postgres RLS, not per endpoint). Add regression tests for those cases plus a broader authz matrix (tenant A token against tenant B resource IDs on every endpoint). Check logs for past exploitation, and if real data leaked, start incident or breach response. Re-run the suite and require zero isolation failures before release. Going forward, report pass rates by severity.
R10: This is a lexical recall failure. Dense embeddings and standard analyzers break up identifiers like "PP-27/2022" and "INV-8841-ID" (the tokenizer splits on - and /, embeddings capture the topic but not the exact string). Fix: detect identifiers in the query with patterns for regulation numbers (PP, UU, Perpres, Permen + number + year) and SKUs, plus normalization (PP 27 Tahun 2022, PP No. 27/2022, and PP-27/2022 all become one canonical form). Index structured fields as keyword fields (regulation_number, sku) with exact and normalized variants, and keep a separate keyword or edge-ngram subfield alongside the Indonesian analyzer (stemmer and stopwords should not touch identifiers). Route identifier queries to an exact-match filter or a strong boost first, then fall back to hybrid (BM25 + vector with RRF). Pin exact matches at the top before the reranker, or use a reranker that doesn't push them down. Respect tenant and ACL filters. Evaluate on a labeled set of exact-ID queries using Recall@5 and MRR, separate from the topical queries.
R11: Don't ship it as the default yet. The average gain hides a regression in a segment that matters: exact-SKU lookups are high-intent queries close to purchase, and a 15% drop there is serious. A 420ms p99 increase likely breaks the latency SLO. Next steps: check significance with confidence intervals (bootstrap over queries) for the overall gain and per segment. Diagnose why the reranker demotes exact matches. Options: route queries detected as identifiers or SKUs around the reranker, or pin exact lexical matches above it. Add exact-match features to the reranker or fine-tune it on those cases. Cut latency by reranking fewer candidates (top-50 down to top-20), using a distilled or quantized model, batching, a timeout with fallback to the first-stage ranking, and caching. Re-evaluate with segment guardrails (no segment regresses more than 2%, p99 within budget) and then run an online A/B test with business metrics. Ship only when all guardrails pass, possibly to non-SKU traffic first.
R12: Converting the PNG won't make it truly sharp. A 512px raster has no vector data. Embedding the PNG in an SVG wrapper changes nothing, and auto-tracing (Potrace, Illustrator Image Trace, vectorizer tools) only approximates the shapes: curves wobble, small text and gradients degrade, and anti-aliased edges create artifacts. Best option: get the original vector source from the designer or brand owner (AI, EPS, PDF, SVG, Figma). Next best: redraw the logo by hand as a vector in Figma, Illustrator, or Inkscape, using the PNG as a guide. Match the brand colors exactly, convert the text to outlines or use the licensed font, and clean up the paths. Auto-trace only for simple flat logos, followed by manual cleanup and a visual diff against the original at large sizes. Then optimize with SVGO, set a viewBox, remove fixed width and height, add a title for accessibility, and test at 16px and at large sizes, on light and dark backgrounds. Check you have the rights to recreate the mark.
